# MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems

Hehai Lin    Qi Yang    Chengwei Qin ^(†)^(†)thanks: Corresponding to
[chengweiqin@hkust-gz.edu.cn](mailto:chengweiqin@hkust-gz.edu.cn)
Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
(Guangzhou) Affiliation: Ant Group

###### Abstract

Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design seeks to learn reusable
orchestration policies, yet prevailing approaches remain largely
one-shot: an Orchestrator generates a system but only observes and
learns from its terminal outcome. This paradigm discards execution
trajectories that expose system-level failures and contain fine-grained
information beyond the terminal outcome, leaving no direct basis for
revising the source MAS, evaluating the updated MAS, or learning from
the resulting contrast. To this end, we introduce MAS-Loop, an
execution-grounded framework that closes this feedback loop by coupling
an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. For each task,
the Orchestrator constructs and executes a source MAS to obtain an
outcome score and an intermediate trajectory. Conditioned on the
trajectory, the Refiner localizes an actionable failure, formulates a
trajectory-grounded diagnosis, and proposes a bounded patch to the
agents, information flow, or execution configuration. The executable
updated MAS is re-executed on the same task to measure its realized
outcome under stochastic execution. This pair-MAS comparison provides
complementary learning signals: the Orchestrator learns to generate
strong systems with fewer recoverable failures, whereas the Refiner
learns to expose and repair observed weaknesses, thereby driving
policy-level co-evolution across training iterations. We evaluate
MAS-Loop across interaction environments, knowledge-intensive multi-hop
reasoning, and general reasoning, examining both the complete framework
and the independent utility of these two policies. Experiments show that
MAS-Loop achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated
baselines, with consistent gains from refinement across all evaluated
benchmarks. The co-evolution process also yields MAS-JudgeCorpus, a
dataset of execution-grounded source-updated pairs with orchestration-
and trajectory-level supervision, which can provide the community with
support for MAS reward modeling and trajectory-aware investigation.

|     |

## 1 Introduction

Training-time multi-agent system (MAS) design has emerged as a promising
alternative to inference-time MAS design, where the workflow search must
be repeated for different tasks and cannot accumulate reusable
experience across tasks ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [Ke et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib9); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib10); [Lin et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib5)). Training-time MAS trains an Orchestrator to
construct a task-specific MAS by selecting models or tools, assigning
agent roles, and organizing communication ([Li et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12); [Ke et al., 2025a](#bib.bib1); [Tran et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3)). The system then executes and uses its outcomes to
improve the Orchestrator through supervised learning ([Ye et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38); [Yue et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)), reinforcement
learning ([Yang and Thomason, 2026](#bib.bib23); [Ke et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)), and graph-based optimization ([Zhuge et al.,
2024](#bib.bib13); [Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)). In this way,
experience acquired from previous executions can be encoded into a
reusable orchestration policy and transferred to future tasks ([Lin et
al., 2026d](#bib.bib37)).

Although this makes MAS construction learnable, this _one-shot
orchestration_ remains an incomplete foundation for effective MAS
self-evolution ([Qi et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)): orchestration and
execution feedback remain disconnected. A system trajectory can expose
missing information flow, redundant reasoning, or failures in
verification and aggregation ([Shen et al., 2025](#bib.bib14); [Cemri et
al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). Yet this trajectory-level evidence is often
omitted from the terminal correctness signal ([Jwalapuram et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26)). Therefore, without a feedback-driven refinement
mechanism, the Orchestrator must discover better designs indirectly
through independently sampled rollouts and their sparse outcome
rewards ([Zhang, 2026](#bib.bib21); [Su et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Lin
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib58); [Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib59)). Although
this trial-and-error process may eventually favor stronger systems, it
relies on vanilla independent rollouts and sparse terminal rewards
rather than utilizing rich intermediate trajectories as feedback to
directly diagnose failures, guide targeted repairs, and optimize from
verified improvements.

![Refer to caption](2610.38946v1/background.png)

Figure 1: The Illustration of MAS-Loop. (a) Existing training-time MAS
methods rely on one-shot orchestration and omit intermediate execution
feedback from optimization. (b) MAS-Loop moves from one-shot
orchestration to execution-grounded adversarial co-evolution by adding a
trajectory-conditioned Refiner and incorporating coupled incentive
learning signals.

However, a complete self-evolution loop requires more than learning to
generate the next system: it should connect execution evidence to a
direct intervention on the current system and facilitate learning based
on the consequences of that intervention ([Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib40); [Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib41)). To this end, we
introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that augments the
_Orchestrator_ with a complementary learned policy, the _Refiner_. The
Orchestrator first constructs a source MAS, whose execution produces a
terminal score and an intermediate trajectory. The Refiner observes the
source design, final prediction, and trajectory to localize actionable
weaknesses, formulate a grounded diagnosis, and propose a bounded patch
to agent roles, information flow, or execution settings. This patch is
compiled into an updated MAS and re-executed on the same task to measure
the realized outcome change. The source-updated score difference
provides coupled learning signals: it encourages the Orchestrator to
produce strong systems with fewer recoverable weaknesses and trains the
Refiner to generate valid revisions that repair observed failures,
enabling the two policies to co-evolve from this rich-learning
closed-loop. This co-evolution occurs across policy-optimization
iterations: each rollout contains one bounded refinement, while
subsequent task rollouts use the newly updated Orchestrator and Refiner.

During policy co-evolution, MAS-Loop naturally produces large numbers of
execution-grounded source-updated pairs. To obtain reliable comparisons,
we retain tasks with a fixed rollout budget, discard ties and pairs with
insufficient absolute or relative score gaps, remove locally
inconsistent examples, and canonicalize Refiner operations before
operation-aware deduplication. The resulting MAS-JudgeCorpus contains
source and updated MAS instances whose quality differences are
established by same-task re-execution, providing pairwise preferences
for training MAS reward models with orchestration- and execution-level
supervision. Then we leverage MAS-JudgeRM for test-time ranking and
selection among candidate MAS, while the retained trajectory evidence
also offers a basis for future trajectory-conditioned judging and other
execution-aware evaluations.

We evaluate MAS-Loop across interaction environments,
knowledge-intensive multi-hop reasoning, and general reasoning,
including both in-task performance and out-of-task transfer. MAS-Loop
achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated
single-agent and automatic MAS baselines. The Orchestrator remains
effective independently, while the Refiner consistently improves both
its source systems and those produced by other MAS methods across
in-task and out-of-task evaluations. For MAS-JudgeCorpus, we train
MAS-JudgeRM on pairwise preferences and compare it with general-purpose
reward models, orchestration-specific reward models, and prompted LLM
judges for selecting among a fixed set of candidate MAS. Together, these
experiments assess both MAS-Loop’s effectiveness as a self-evolving MAS
framework and MAS-JudgeCorpus’s value for test-time MAS selection. Our
contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We identify a central limitation of current training-time MAS:
  one-shot orchestration leaves execution feedback disconnected from the
  MAS design, forcing the Orchestrator to improve indirectly through
  sparse terminal rewards rather than direct rich trajectory-level
  evidence.
- •
  We introduce MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that couples an
  Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner. The paired
  re-execution evaluates the updated MAS under the same task protocol
  and provides complementary learning signals that drive both policies
  to co-evolve across training iterations.
- •
  We construct MAS-JudgeCorpus from execution-grounded source–updated
  MAS pairs, applying fixed-rollout quality filtering, conservative
  consistency checks, and operation-aware deduplication to obtain
  reliable preferences for training MAS reward models.

## 2 Related Work

### 2.1 Automatic Multi-Agent System Design

Inference-time MAS design typically uses a powerful frontier LLM
together with iterative search, reflection, or optimization to construct
an agent workflow for each task ([Ruan et al., 2026](#bib.bib27); [Ma et
al., 2026](#bib.bib42); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib43)). This approach
can adapt the workflow to different tasks, but the search usually has to
be repeated when the domain changes. It therefore has limited ability to
accumulate orchestration experience that transfers across tasks ([Lin et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib4); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib44); [Xu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib45)). Training-time MAS design instead learns an
orchestration policy, often implemented with a smaller model, from
experience collected across prior executions ([Su et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39); [Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib49)). Existing studies
explore supervised learning from successful orchestration traces ([Wang
et al., 2025](#bib.bib48); [Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib46)),
reinforcement learning with task-level rewards and structured credit
assignment ([Ke et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Chen et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib29)), and graph-based optimization of agent organizations
and communication patterns ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib47); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib50)). Despite this progress, most training-time approaches
remain largely one-shot. They use execution outcomes to improve later
orchestration proposals, but do not closely connect trajectory-level
feedback to the decisions that created the system and lack a direct
refinement mechanism. So the Orchestrator must discover better designs
indirectly through repeated rollouts and sparse outcome rewards.

MAS-Loop addresses this limitation by coupling the Orchestrator with a
trajectory-conditioned Refiner, which uses evidence from the source
MAS’s execution to generate an executable revision. The updated MAS is
then re-executed on the same task, and the score difference between the
source and updated systems provides adversarial learning signals for the
co-evolution of both policies.

### 2.2 Multi-Agent System Benchmarks

Existing MAS benchmarks characterize several aspects of multi-agent
behavior. MultiAgentBench measures collaboration and competition among
agents under different interaction settings ([Zhu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25); [Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib57)), while other work
organizes recurring coordination failures or attributes errors to
particular agents and interactions ([Ge et al., 2026](#bib.bib32); [Kong
et al., 2026](#bib.bib31); [Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)).
Complementary metrics and reward-modeling approaches assess the quality
of multi-agent organizations by comparing orchestration choices or
scoring system behaviors and trajectories ([Tsang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30)). However, these resources primarily characterize MAS
behavior or score existing designs, providing limited paired supervision
that connects execution evidence to a concrete system revision. In this
work, MAS-JudgeCorpus is constructed from source MAS and
trajectory-conditioned updates generated during MAS-Loop, with same-task
re-execution establishing their relative quality. After retaining
fixed-budget tasks with sufficiently large, non-tied absolute and
relative score gaps, removing pair-level ties and locally inconsistent
comparisons, canonicalizing Refiner operations, and deduplicating by
task-operation pairs, the corpus provides complementary pairwise
supervision at two levels for training MAS reward models:
orchestration-level supervision uses task descriptions and MAS graph
structure to support execution-free judgment, whereas trajectory-level
supervision additionally incorporates rich execution evidence for more
accurate quality assessment.

## 3 MAS-Loop: Execution-Grounded Adversarial Co-Evolution

### 3.1 Overview

![Refer to caption](2610.38946v1/method.png)

Figure 2: Overview of MAS-Loop. The paired source and updated MAS’s
material provide complementary rewards that update both policies,
closing the feedback loop from execution back to subsequent MAS
construction.

Given a task instance $`x`$, our goal is to learn two coupled policies:
an Orchestrator that constructs an executable source MAS and a Refiner
that diagnoses its execution and applies a bounded revision. We
represent an MAS as an attributed directed graph

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       M=(V,E,\phi),
       ```            |     | (1) |

where $`V`$ is the set of agents, $`E\subseteq V\times V`$ specifies
directed communication and dependency relations, and $`\phi`$ assigns
each agent its role and execution configuration. Thus, $`M`$ specifies
which agents participate, how they are connected, and what function each
agent performs. An executor $`\mathcal{E}`$ instantiates the graph on
the task:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
(\tau,y)\sim\mathcal{E}(M,x),\qquad s=r_{\mathrm{term}}(x,y,y^{\star}),
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\tau`$ records node-level responses, dependency usage,
intermediate evidence, and execution failures; $`y`$ is the final
prediction; $`y^{\star}`$ is the task’s gold label; and
$`r_{\mathrm{term}}`$ computes the terminal reward from the prediction
and the task outcome criterion. The scalar $`s`$ summarizes the final
task outcome and is retained by the training-side evaluator for reward
computation only. In contrast, $`\tau`$ preserves the execution evidence
needed to identify where the realized execution may have failed.
MAS-Loop couples the two policies through an execution-grounded revision
loop: the Orchestrator $`\pi_{\mathrm{O}}`$ first generates a source MAS
$`M_{\mathrm{src}}`$, after which the Refiner $`\pi_{\mathrm{R}}`$ uses
the execution evidence to produce a structured diagnosis $`g`$ and a
bounded patch $`p`$, jointly denoted by $`a_{\mathrm{R}}=(g,p)`$.
Applying $`p`$ yields an updated MAS $`M_{\mathrm{upd}}`$ for
re-execution, which establishes the credit-assignment boundary: the
Orchestrator is trained according to the quality and refinability of its
source MAS, whereas the Refiner is trained according to the realized
score change following its diagnosis and patch.

### 3.2 Structured Policy Interfaces

Orchestrator. The Orchestrator receives the task $`x`$ and samples a
source MAS

|     |                                                    |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       M_{\mathrm{src}}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{O}}(\cdot\mid x).
       ```                                                 |     | (3) |

Rather than answering $`x`$ directly, the Orchestrator instantiates a
task-specific computational organization. It assigns complementary
responsibilities and execution configurations to the agents in $`V`$,
and uses the directed edges in $`E`$ to determine how intermediate
results flow between them. A typical source MAS therefore decomposes the
task across upstream agents, passes their relevant outputs to downstream
agents, and uses the resulting dependency structure to produce the final
response.

Refiner. After the source MAS is executed, the source system and its
execution record are packaged into a bounded diagnostic input

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
d_{\mathrm{src}}=\mathcal{D}(x,M_{\mathrm{src}},\tau_{\mathrm{src}},y_{\mathrm{src}}),
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\mathcal{D}`$ packages the task, source MAS, execution
trajectory, and final prediction. It explicitly removes the gold label,
so the Refiner must decide how to edit the source MAS from observable
execution evidence rather than an oracle correctness bit. Given this
input, the Refiner produces

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
a_{\mathrm{R}}=(g,p)\sim\pi_{\mathrm{R}}(\cdot\mid x,d_{\mathrm{src}}),
``` |  | (5) |

where $`g`$ is a structured diagnosis and $`p`$ is a bounded patch; the
Refiner outputs them together in one step. The diagnosis localizes an
actionable failure, states a causal hypothesis, and proposes a repair
plan supported by trajectory references. We organize the operation space
according to the aspect of the source MAS being revised. The four
categories below together define the Refiner action space:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{preserve}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{\mathrm{Accept}\},`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{agent}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{\mathrm{AddAgent},\ \mathrm{RewriteRole}\},`$ |  | (6) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{flow}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{\mathrm{AddEdge},\ \mathrm{RemoveEdge}\},`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{adapt}}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{\mathrm{AdjustReasoningBudget},\ \mathrm{ChangeTool}\}.`$ |  |  |

Operation space. *(1) Preservation.* $`\mathrm{Accept}`$ keeps the
source MAS unchanged when its execution is adequate or when the
diagnostic evidence does not justify a reliable intervention. *(2) Agent
organization.* $`\mathrm{AddAgent}`$ introduces a new task-solving agent
and, as part of this atomic operation, connects its output to the
current aggregation agent without changing the aggregation agent itself.
$`\mathrm{RewriteRole}`$ revises an existing agent whose responsibility
is misaligned with its subtask. *(3) Information flow.*
$`\mathrm{AddEdge}`$ instantiates a new dependency between agents,
whereas $`\mathrm{RemoveEdge}`$ eliminates an irrelevant or harmful
dependency. The compiler rejects any edit that produces an unresolved
endpoint, a cycle, or an executable graph without a valid path to
aggregation. *(4) Execution adaptation.*
$`\mathrm{AdjustReasoningBudget}`$ changes an agent’s explicitly
scalable reasoning depth, such as the number of search rounds or its
generation allowance, while $`\mathrm{ChangeTool}`$ enables, disables,
or switches the tool access assigned to an agent when its capabilities
do not match the subtask. A deterministic patch compiler applies the
canonicalized operations to obtain the updated MAS

|     |                                                   |     |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       M_{\mathrm{upd}}=\mathcal{C}(M_{\mathrm{src}},p).
       ```                                                |     | (7) |

Pair Data Collection. For each source sample, the executor produces

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\tau_{\mathrm{src}},y_{\mathrm{src}})\sim\mathcal{E}(M_{\mathrm{src}},x),\qquad s_{\mathrm{src}}=r_{\mathrm{term}}(x,y_{\mathrm{src}},y^{\star}),
``` |  | (8) |

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\tau_{\mathrm{upd}},y_{\mathrm{upd}})\sim\mathcal{E}(M_{\mathrm{upd}},x),\qquad s_{\mathrm{upd}}=r_{\mathrm{term}}(x,y_{\mathrm{upd}},y^{\star}).
``` |  | (9) |

We re-execute the unchanged source graph when the Refiner abstains or
produces an invalid patch. For every task, the training group contains
multiple independently sampled source-updated rollout pairs. Each source
MAS receives one Refiner decision and one independent updated execution;
the group therefore estimates refinement behavior across sampled systems
rather than repeatedly evaluating the same patch.

### 3.3 Adversarial Co-Evolution

The paired records provide a stochastic, execution-grounded signal of
whether a Refiner intervention is useful. For an individual rollout, the
difference below is a realized score change

|     |                                             |     |      |
|-----|---------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta s=s_{\mathrm{upd}}-s_{\mathrm{src}}.
       ```                                          |     | (10) |

This quantity is then used to construct complementary rewards for the
two policies. For the Orchestrator, the reward is defined as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{\mathrm{O}}=\begin{cases}s_{\mathrm{src}},&\text{if }M_{\mathrm{upd}}=M_{\mathrm{src}},\\
s_{\mathrm{src}}-\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}\max(\Delta s,0),&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}\geq 0`$ controls the strength of the
adversarial penalty. For an unchanged MAS, any score difference caused
by re-execution is not used to modify the Orchestrator reward. For a
valid update, the first term favors source systems that solve the task
without refinement, while the second term penalizes only positive
improvements: a successful repair indicates that the source system
contains a recoverable weakness, whereas a harmful intervention reflects
a failure of the Refiner rather than an additional weakness of the
source system.

For the Refiner, an *Accept* action is evaluated by whether the source
system is already correct, while an executable intervention is rewarded
according to its measured improvement. Let
$`c_{\mathrm{src}}\in\{+1,-1\}`$ indicate whether the source answer
satisfies the task criterion. We define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{\mathrm{R}}=\begin{cases}-\eta,&\text{if invalid,or if }a_{\mathrm{R}}=\mathrm{Accept}\text{ and }c_{\mathrm{src}}=-1,\\
+\eta,&\text{if }a_{\mathrm{R}}=\mathrm{Accept}\text{ and }c_{\mathrm{src}}=+1,\\
\Delta s,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}
``` |  | (12) |

where $`\eta>0`$ sets both the invalid-action penalty and the magnitude
of the accept reward. Thus, a positive $`\Delta s`$ rewards a repair
that improves the re-executed system, whereas a negative $`\Delta s`$
penalizes a damaging intervention. The signed reward for
$`\mathrm{Accept}`$ guides the Refiner both to preserve a source MAS
that is already correct and to avoid accepting one that remains
incorrect. We use $`\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}=0.3`$ and $`\eta=0.5`$ by
default, and we study the effect of these two hyperparameters in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Results and Analysis ‣ 4 Main Experiments ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems").

Together, these rewards define a constructive adversarial objective. The
Orchestrator learns to construct source systems that are effective from
the outset and require little or no further refinement, while the
Refiner learns to identify grounded interventions that improve observed
systems.

GRPO-based co-evolution. We use Group Relative Policy Optimization
(GRPO) as the standard policy-optimization procedure ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib33); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib51)). For each policy, we
combine sampled rollout records with their corresponding rewards to form
separate training batches:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{O}}=\left\{\left(\zeta_{\mathrm{O}}^{(i)},r_{\mathrm{O}}^{(i)}\right)\right\}_{i=1}^{N},\qquad\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{R}}=\left\{\left(\zeta_{\mathrm{R}}^{(j)},r_{\mathrm{R}}^{(j)}\right)\right\}_{j=1}^{N},
``` |  | (13) |

where $`\zeta_{\mathrm{O}}`$ and $`\zeta_{\mathrm{R}}`$ denote rollout
records sampled for the Orchestrator and Refiner, respectively. We apply
GRPO separately to these two batches using their corresponding rewards:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\pi_{\mathrm{O}}^{k}\leftarrow\operatorname{GRPO}(\pi_{\mathrm{O}}^{k-1};\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{O}}^{k}),\qquad\pi_{\mathrm{R}}^{k}\leftarrow\operatorname{GRPO}(\pi_{\mathrm{R}}^{k-1};\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{R}}^{k}).
``` |  | (14) |

## 4 Main Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks. We evaluate MAS-Loop on three task families: interaction
environment, multi-hop question answering, and general reasoning. The
Orchestrator and Refiner are trained on ALFWorld ([Shridhar et al.,
2020](#bib.bib19)), HotpotQA ([Yang et al., 2018](#bib.bib18)), and
DeepScaler ([Tan et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)). We evaluate in-task
performance on ALFWorld, HotpotQA, and AIME ([MAA-Committees,
2025](#bib.bib15)) and test out-of-task (OOT) generalization on
SciWorld ([Wang et al., 2022a](#bib.bib20)), VitaBench ([He et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52)), BrowseComp-Plus ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)),
and GPQA-Diamond ([Rein et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)). All metrics are
converted to a common $`0-100\%`$ scale.
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Statistics of Benchmarks ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
provides additional information about the datasets, splits, and
evaluation procedures.

Baselines. We compare MAS-Loop against three families of baselines. The
first family contains general inference baselines, including
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib35)) and
self-consistency decoding (CoT-SC) ([Wang et al., 2022b](#bib.bib36)).
The second family contains inference-time workflow-construction methods,
including AFlow ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)), AOrchestra ([Ruan et
al., 2026](#bib.bib27)), and Skill-MAS ([Lin et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib37)). The third family contains training-time
coordination methods, including MAS-GPT ([Ye et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)),
ToolOrchestra ([Su et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)), and MAS-Orchestra ([Ke et
al., 2026](#bib.bib22)). Baseline details are elaborated in
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Baselines ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems").
Across all experiments, we additionally evaluate the independent
deployment ability of Orchestrator and Refiner. We leverage
Qwen3-8B ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib28)) as the trainable Orchestrator and
Refiner, and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib28)) as
the frozen sub-agent backbone. Detailed implementation and adaptation
settings are provided in
Appendix [C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems").

|  | MAS-Orchestra | 14.42 | 4.33 | 19.38 | 48.00 | 12.50 | 21.05 | 49.49 | 24.17 |
|  |    + Refiner | 18.59 | 9.30 | 23.54 | 58.00 | 13.69 | 24.56 | 59.09 | 29.54 (+5.37) |
| MAS-Loop | Orchestrator | 56.41 | 21.17 | 30.49 | 63.00 | 13.00 | 45.61 | 60.61 | 41.47 |
|  |    + Refiner | 56.73 | 22.87 | 35.47 | 64.50 | 15.48 | 47.37 | 61.62 | 43.43 (+1.96) |

Table 1: Quantification comparison of MAS-Loop and baselines across
three train-test transfer settings. “OOT” denotes evaluation on an
out-of-task dataset not used for training. ALFW: ALFWorld, SciW:
ScienceWorld, VITA: VitaBench, BCP: BrowseComp-Plus, GPQA: GPQA-Diamond.
Avg. reports average performance, and Bold denotes the best result.

Main results. First, existing MAS baselines do not exhibit a stable
advantage over single-agent reasoning across task families. Their
relative rankings vary substantially across datasets: for example,
AOrchestra markedly outperforms CoT-SC on ALFWorld ($`57.69\%`$ vs.
$`32.69\%`$), yet falls well below it on VITA ($`8.49\%`$ vs.
$`32.02\%`$). The aggregate results reinforce this lack of consistency:
among the six unrefined MAS baselines, five underperform CoT-SC on Avg,
and four even fall below CoT. This pattern is consistent with prior
findings that automatically constructed MAS often fail to yield robust
gains over strong single-agent systems because architectural and
coordination failures can offset their potential benefits ([Jwalapuram
et al., 2026](#bib.bib26); [Cemri et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)). In
contrast, MAS-Loop delivers the strongest overall performance,
outperforming both single-agent baselines and competing MAS methods
across nearly all evaluated datasets. The breadth of these gains
suggests that execution-grounded feedback and co-evolution provide a
more reliable learning signal than one-shot orchestration alone.

Second, the two learned policies remain effective beyond their joint
deployment. The Orchestrator alone constructs strong source systems,
while coupling it with the Refiner yields further gains. The Refiner is
independent and not tied to its co-trained Orchestrator: when applied
post hoc to MAS generated by Skill-MAS, MAS-GPT, and MAS-Orchestra, it
consistently improves their average performance. Together, these results
show that MAS-Loop learns both a capable standalone orchestration policy
and a transferable refinement policy that generalizes across MAS design
methods.

Figure 3: Reward-coefficient ablations on HotpotQA and out-of-task
BrowseComp-Plus (BCP). Each panel varies one coefficient while holding
the other at its default value.

Ablation Study.
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Results and Analysis ‣ 4 Main Experiments ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
examines the sensitivity of MAS-Loop to its two reward coefficients on
HotpotQA and the out-of-task BrowseComp-Plus benchmark. We vary one
coefficient at a time while fixing the other at its default value, with
all remaining training and evaluation settings held constant. Across
both sweeps, the strongest results concentrate at moderate coefficient
values, whereas the endpoints perform less favorably and occasionally
exhibit sharp declines. For $`\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}`$, the
$`\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}=0`$ endpoint removes the coupled penalty and
performs below the default setting, directly showing that source-only
optimization does not recover the benefit of coupled learning. For both
$`\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}}`$ and $`\eta`$, introducing moderate
adversarial pressure improves both in-task and transfer performance, but
an overly large value substantially degrades both, suggesting that
excessive pressure can compromise the Orchestrator’s source-quality
objective.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
further includes a rollout-execution-matched comparison that increases
the rollout budget of MAS-Orchestra, a one-step prompted self-reflection
control, and a base-model scaling study that replaces Qwen3-8B with
Qwen3-14B for both the Orchestrator and Refiner. Together, these
ablation studies provide further evidence to support the effectiveness
of MAS-Loop.

## 5 MAS-JudgeCorpus

Beyond policy learning, the execution-grounded rollouts produced by
MAS-Loop provide direct preference supervision for evaluating MAS
designs. We organize these paired rollouts into MAS-JudgeCorpus and use
them to train a reward model, MAS-JudgeRM, for test-time candidate
selection. Our primary setting ranks candidate systems at the
orchestration level, while a trajectory-conditioned variant quantifies
the additional value of execution evidence.

### 5.1 MAS-JudgeCorpus Construction

Raw rollout pairs. MAS-JudgeCorpus is constructed from the
source-updated MAS pairs generated during HotpotQA training (10000
tasks). Each rollout executes both systems on the same task, producing a
locally comparable outcome pair together with their execution evidence.
These rollout-level pairs are the basic units where the final preference
examples are selected.

Task-level preference estimation. Because an individual rollout can be
affected by stochastic execution, we aggregate source and updated scores
across all rollouts of the same task to obtain a more reliable
preference direction. We compute
$`\Delta_{\mathrm{task}}=S_{\mathrm{upd}}-S_{\mathrm{src}}`$ and its
relative magnitude
$`g_{\mathrm{rel}}=|\Delta_{\mathrm{task}}|/\min(S_{\mathrm{src}},S_{\mathrm{upd}})`$,
then discard ties and tasks with an absolute gap below $`2.0`$ or a
relative gap below $`25\%`$. Both thresholds must be satisfied. If
$`\min(S_{\mathrm{src}},S_{\mathrm{upd}})=0`$, while the relative gap is
undefined, the task is excluded by the $`\Delta_{\mathrm{task}}`$
threshold. This retains 2,063 tasks with a clear aggregate preference.

Rollout-level example construction. We then return to the individual
rollout pairs within the retained tasks, removing pair-level ties and
pairs whose local score direction conflicts with the aggregate
task-level preference. Thus, task-level aggregation is used only to
stabilize preference assignment, while every final sample remains a
rollout-level source-updated comparison: the higher-scoring system is
labeled chosen and the other rejected. After mapping legacy aliases to
the seven canonical Refiner operations and retaining at most one rollout
pair per task and canonicalized operation signature, we obtain 8,223
trajectory pairs.

### 5.2 Test-Time Selection Experiment

#### 5.2.1 Experimental Setup

Protocol. We evaluate whether MAS-JudgeCorpus can support test-time MAS
selection in a fixed best-of-$`16`$ setting. For each held-out task, a
shared generator produces 16 candidate MAS designs, and every
verification method receives the same pool. Each method ranks these
candidates and adopts the answer from the selected MAS as the final
prediction. Consequently, performance differences reflect verification
quality rather than candidate generation. MAS-JudgeRM is trained on
MAS-JudgeCorpus using a Bradley-Terry objective. Its orchestration-level
variant observes only the task and candidate design, while its
trajectory-level variant additionally receives execution evidence.

Evaluation. We report final-answer accuracy on HotpotQA and the
out-of-task BrowseComp-Plus (BCP), together with the method-specific
verification tokens. Comparisons include Orchestrator, Majority Voting,
and Oracle, as well as prompted LLM judges and general-purpose or
orchestration-specific reward models. The Oracle selects a correct
candidate whenever the fixed pool contains one, while all other methods
operate without ground-truth labels. We also evaluate
trajectory-conditioned variants of DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MAS-JudgeRM to
investigate the value of execution evidence.

#### 5.2.2 Results and Analysis

|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Category | Method | Verification Level | HotpotQA |  | BCP_(OOT) |  |
|  |  |  | Acc | \#Token (M) | Acc | \#Token (M) |
| Baseline | Orchestrator (LB) | \- | 53.00 | \- | 7.74 | \- |
|  | Majority Voting | \- | 55.50 | \- | 11.90 | \- |
|  | Oracle (UB) | \- | 77.00 | \- | 26.79 | \- |
| LLM-as-a-Judge | Kimi-K3 | Orchestration | 53.00 | 2.46 | 14.29 | 3.02 |
|  | Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B | Orchestration | 58.00 | 2.72 | 15.48 | 3.50 |
|  | DeepSeek-V4-Flash | Orchestration | 51.50 | 2.47 | 14.88 | 3.12 |
|  |  | Trajectory | 60.00 | 8.88 | 20.83 | 12.47 |

Table 2: Test-time MAS selection from a shared best-of-16 candidate
pool. Orchestrator (LB) and Oracle (UB) denote the performance lower and
upper bounds, respectively.

Orchestration-level verification. MAS-JudgeRM consistently outperforms
both reward-model baselines on HotpotQA and BCP. However, it does not
consistently match the strongest prompted LLM judges: it narrowly trails
the best LLM judge on HotpotQA and falls behind all three on BCP. This
contrast exposes a limitation of architecture-only verification. A
serialized MAS design specifies roles, tools, and topology, but provides
little evidence of how the system will actually behave. With only this
limited structural evidence, even a compact reward model trained
specifically for MAS evaluation cannot match the predictive reasoning
capabilities of much larger frontier LLM.

Trajectory-level verification. The comparison changes substantially once
execution evidence is available. MAS-JudgeRM reaches $`60.00\%`$ on
HotpotQA, matching the trajectory-conditioned DeepSeek-V4-Flash judge,
and achieves $`22.62\%`$ on BCP, surpassing DeepSeek’s $`20.83\%`$.
These results show that a compact reward model trained on
execution-grounded preferences can serve as an effective MAS judge when
it can inspect how the candidate actually executes. Although
trajectory-level verification requires roughly four times the token
overhead, its stronger in-task and transfer performance highlights the
importance of execution evidence for reliable MAS evaluation.
Orchestration-only judging remains cheaper but is intrinsically more
limited.

## 6 Conclusion

In this work, we propose MAS-Loop, an execution-grounded framework that
couples an Orchestrator with a trajectory-conditioned Refiner to close
the feedback loop between MAS construction, execution, and revision.
Paired re-execution provides complementary learning signals that
encourage strong source systems and effective bounded refinements.
Experiments show that MAS-Loop improves over one-shot MAS orchestration,
while both policies remain useful independently and the Refiner is easy
and effective to transfer to other MAS generators. The resulting pair
rollouts also form MAS-JudgeCorpus for training MAS-JudgeRM, whose
results highlight the importance of execution evidence for reliable MAS
evaluation. Together, these findings offer insights into building
effective self-evolving MAS by moving beyond one-shot orchestration
toward a more targeted and precise loop of system generation,
execution-grounded refinement, and policy-level co-evolution across
training iterations.

## Ethics Statement

This work follows the ICLR Code of Ethics and studies automated MAS
construction and refinement in controlled research benchmarks. We do not
collect new human-subject, personal, or sensitive data, and our
experiments use established research datasets and model-generated
execution trajectories. The study focuses on general reasoning, question
answering, and benchmarked interactive tasks rather than decisions about
individuals or demographic groups, and no component is designed to
target or disadvantage any population. We use all datasets in accordance
with their intended research settings and licenses, and report our
methodology and experimental results with an emphasis on transparency
and reproducibility.

## Reproducibility Statement

Our reinforcement-learning implementation is built with verl.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B MAS-Loop Algorithm ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
provides the complete MAS-Loop procedure, while
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
documents benchmark protocols, baselines, model configurations,
optimization hyperparameters, and hardware.
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Prompt ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
further reports the structured prompts and output formats used by the
Orchestrator, Refiner, and LLM judges. We use fixed evaluation settings
for controlled comparisons, and the supplementary code supports
reproducibility.

## LLM Usage

Separate from the language models evaluated in our experiments, LLM
assistants are used during manuscript preparation for writing and
presentation: improving grammar, clarity, organization, and LaTeX
formatting without changing the underlying experimental evidence. All
assisted text is manually reviewed by the authors, and the authors
remain responsible for the final content.

## Appendix A Appendix Overview

This appendix complements the main paper with methodological and
experimental details.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B MAS-Loop Algorithm ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
presents the complete MAS-Loop training procedure.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
documents the benchmarks, baselines, and implementation settings, while
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
reports the rollout-execution-matched, prompted self-reflection, and
base-model scaling ablations.
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Case Study ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
illustrates how trajectory-grounded refinement changes an executed MAS,
and
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Prompt ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
provides the prompt contracts and structured output formats used by each
model component.

## Appendix B MAS-Loop Algorithm

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix B MAS-Loop Algorithm ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
summarizes the execution-grounded co-evolution procedure and makes the
credit-assignment boundary between the two policies explicit. In each
rollout, the Orchestrator constructs a source MAS, whose execution is
converted into a bounded diagnostic input for the Refiner. The Refiner
either accepts the source system or proposes a patch that is compiled
and validated before re-execution. The paired outcomes determine
policy-specific rewards: the Orchestrator is trained on source quality
and recoverable weaknesses, whereas the Refiner is trained on the
realized score change following its action.

0:  Labeled task batch $`\mathcal{X}=\{(x,y^{\star})\}`$ and rollouts
per task $`G`$

0:  Policies $`\pi_{\mathrm{O}},\pi_{\mathrm{R}}`$, diagnostic
constructor $`\mathcal{D}`$, patch compiler $`\mathcal{C}`$, executor
$`\mathcal{E}`$, evaluator $`r_{\mathrm{term}}`$, and reward
coefficients $`\lambda_{\mathrm{adv}},\eta`$

0:  Co-evolved policies $`\pi_{\mathrm{O}}`$ and $`\pi_{\mathrm{R}}`$

1:  for each training iteration $`k`$ do

2:   Initialize rollout batches
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{O}}\leftarrow\varnothing`$ and
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{R}}\leftarrow\varnothing`$.

3:   for each task $`(x,y^{\star})\in\mathcal{X}`$ do

4:    for each rollout $`m\in\{1,\ldots,G\}`$ do

5:     Sample and validate
$`M_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)}\sim\pi_{\mathrm{O}}(\cdot\mid x)`$.

6:     Execute
$`(\tau_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},y_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)})\sim\mathcal{E}(M_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},x)`$.

7:     Construct the gold-free observation
$`d_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)}=\mathcal{D}(x,M_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},\tau_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},y_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)})`$.

8:     Sample
$`a_{\mathrm{R}}^{(x,m)}=(g^{(x,m)},p^{(x,m)})\sim\pi_{\mathrm{R}}(\cdot\mid x,d_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)})`$.

9:     Privately set
$`s_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)}=r_{\mathrm{term}}(x,y_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},y^{\star})`$
in the trainer after sampling $`a_{\mathrm{R}}^{(x,m)}`$.

10:     if $`a_{\mathrm{R}}^{(x,m)}=\mathrm{Accept}`$ then

11:      Set
$`M_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)}\leftarrow M_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)}`$.

12:     else

13:      Compile and validate
$`M_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)}\leftarrow\mathcal{C}(M_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},p^{(x,m)})`$.

14:      if $`M_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)}`$ is not executable then

15:       Mark the update invalid and set
$`M_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)}\leftarrow M_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)}`$ for
re-execution.

16:      end if

17:     end if

18:     Execute
$`(\tau_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)},y_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)})\sim\mathcal{E}(M_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)},x)`$.

19:     Set
$`s_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)}=r_{\mathrm{term}}(x,y_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)},y^{\star})`$
and
$`\Delta s^{(x,m)}=s_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)}-s_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)}`$.

20:     Compute $`r_{\mathrm{O}}^{(x,m)}`$ and
$`r_{\mathrm{R}}^{(x,m)}`$ using
Eqs. equation [11](#S3.E11 "In 3.3 Adversarial Co-Evolution ‣ 3 MAS-Loop: Execution-Grounded Adversarial Co-Evolution ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")–equation [12](#S3.E12 "In 3.3 Adversarial Co-Evolution ‣ 3 MAS-Loop: Execution-Grounded Adversarial Co-Evolution ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems").

21:     Form
$`z^{(x,m)}=(x,M_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},\tau_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},s_{\mathrm{src}}^{(x,m)},a_{\mathrm{R}}^{(x,m)},M_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)},\tau_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)},s_{\mathrm{upd}}^{(x,m)})`$.

22:     Append the policy-specific views of $`z^{(x,m)}`$ and their
rewards to $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{O}}`$ and
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{R}}`$.

23:    end for

24:   end for

25:   Update $`\pi_{\mathrm{O}}`$ with GRPO on
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{O}}`$ and $`\pi_{\mathrm{R}}`$ with GRPO on
$`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{R}}`$.

26:  end for

27:  return Co-evolved policies $`\pi_{\mathrm{O}}`$ and
$`\pi_{\mathrm{R}}`$.

Algorithm 1 Execution-grounded co-evolution in MAS-Loop

benchmark is never used to update or select the Orchestra trained on the
paired source task.

### C.1 Statistics of Benchmarks

Table [3](#A3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
summarizes the role of every benchmark in the experiments. ALFWorld,
HotpotQA, and DeepScaler provide the three training resources for
interaction environment, multi-hop question answering, and general
reasoning, respectively. Their corresponding in-task test sets measure
whether the learned policies retain performance in the task family used
during training. SciWorld, VitaBench, BrowseComp-Plus, and GPQA-Diamond
are held-out out-of-task (OOT) benchmarks and therefore test transfer to
a related but distinct task distribution.

Interaction environments. ALFWorld aligns abstract text environments
with embodied household tasks, allowing an agent to learn and execute
the same high-level task through language actions ([Shridhar et al.,
2020](#bib.bib19)). Its tasks require long-horizon planning, object
manipulation, and adaptation to different household layouts, making it a
natural training and in-task evaluation environment for interactive
agents. SciWorld requires the agent to inspect objects, perform
experiments through sequential actions, and infer the scientific
outcome ([Wang et al., 2022a](#bib.bib20)). VitaBench evaluates
multi-turn tool-using agents in real-world service scenarios, including
food delivery, in-store consumption, and online travel ([He et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52)). It exposes agents to changing user intentions,
interdependent tool calls, and dynamic service states, thereby testing
practical decision-making and recovery over extended interactions.

Knowledge-intensive QA. HotpotQA is a Wikipedia-based multi-hop
question-answering dataset whose questions require combining evidence
from multiple documents ([Yang et al., 2018](#bib.bib18)).
BrowseComp-Plus evaluates deep-research agents over a fixed and curated
document corpus, providing a reproducible alternative to evaluation
against the continuously changing open web ([Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)). Its questions require iterative retrieval, source
comparison, and evidence synthesis, which makes it suitable for
measuring transfer from standard multi-hop QA to more complex
deep-research tasks.

General Reasoning. The DeepScaler training set consists of
competition-style mathematical problems collected for
reinforcement-learning-based reasoning training ([Tan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34)). These problems demand multi-step derivations but
retain verifiable final answers, allowing them to provide training tasks
with reliable outcome-based rewards. AIME is a complex mathematics
competition that typically requires substantial algebraic, geometric,
combinatorial, or number-theoretic reasoning ([MAA-Committees,
2025](#bib.bib15)). GPQA-Diamond comprises expert-written graduate-level
questions in biology, physics, and chemistry, which evaluate scientific
reasoning and domain knowledge outside the mathematical distribution
used for training ([Rein et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)).

### C.2 Baselines

#### C.2.1 MAS-Loop

The main experiment compares MAS-Loop with three types of MAS methods.
For each training-time MAS baseline, we evaluate both its original
Orchestrator and the same Orchestrator augmented with our Refiner
interface where applicable. This controlled adaptation separates
improvements due to the underlying orchestration policy from
improvements due to execution-grounded refinement.

General inference methods. CoT elicits intermediate reasoning steps
before producing the final answer ([Wei et al., 2022](#bib.bib35)).
CoT-SC samples multiple reasoning traces and selects the answer with the
highest consistency ([Wang et al., 2022b](#bib.bib36)). These methods do
not construct an explicit MAS and therefore provide single-agent
inference baselines.

Inference-time MAS methods. AFlow searches over code-represented agentic
workflows using Monte Carlo Tree search ([Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7)). AOrchestra creates task-specific sub-agents by
configuring their instructions, context, tools, and models at inference
time ([Ruan et al., 2026](#bib.bib27)). Skill-MAS records orchestration
experience in an evolvable meta-skill and uses this experience to
construct task-specific MAS workflows ([Lin et al., 2026d](#bib.bib37)).
These methods optimize or instantiate the workflow during inference but
do not train a reusable orchestration policy under our task-specific
training protocol.

Training-time MAS methods. MAS-GPT trains an LLM to generate an
executable, query-adaptive MAS in a single inference ([Ye et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38)). ToolOrchestra learns to coordinate models and tools
through reinforcement learning under effectiveness and efficiency
objectives ([Su et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)). MAS-Orchestra learns
holistic function-calling-based orchestration for generating a complete
MAS ([Ke et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)). These methods are the closest
comparison group because they learn reusable coordination behavior
during training. However, their original formulations do not learn a
trajectory-conditioned policy that directly revises and re-executes the
generated source MAS.

#### C.2.2 MAS-JudgeCorpus

The MAS-JudgeCorpus experiment evaluates test-time MAS selection under a
fixed best-of-$`16`$ protocol. Every verification method receives the
same candidate pool and ranks its candidates without changing the
generator; the answer associated with the selected MAS becomes the final
prediction. Orchestration-level methods observe the task and MAS design,
whereas trajectory-level methods additionally receive execution
evidence.

General baselines. Orchestrator uses an answer produced without
test-time candidate verification and therefore serves as the performance
lower bound. Majority Voting aggregates the answers of the 16 candidates
without learning an explicit quality score. Oracle accesses their
ground-truth correctness and returns a correct answer whenever the pool
contains one, providing the performance upper bound for the fixed
candidate set.

LLM-as-a-Judge baselines. DeepSeek-V4-Flash ([Xu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib53)), Kimi-K3 ([Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib54)), and
Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B rank candidate MAS designs through prompted inference
rather than a separately trained reward model. All three are evaluated
at the orchestration level, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash is additionally
evaluated with trajectory evidence to measure the benefit of observing
execution behavior.

Reward-model baselines. Skywork-V2-Qwen3-8B provides a general-purpose
reward-model reference ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib55)), while Orch-RM
is trained specifically to score MAS organizations ([Tsang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30)). We compare them with MAS-JudgeRM, trained on the
execution-grounded source–updated preferences in MAS-JudgeCorpus.
MAS-JudgeRM is evaluated with both orchestration- and trajectory-level
inputs, allowing us to compare specialized preference supervision
against existing reward models and to isolate the additional value of
execution evidence.

### C.3 Implementation Details

Table [4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ C.3 Implementation Details ‣ Appendix C Experimental Details ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
summarizes key hyperparameters used in our reinforcement learning. The
Orchestrator and Refiner are initialized from Qwen3-8B ([Team,
2025](#bib.bib28)), and updated from separate rollout records using
their respective rewards. Their outputs follow the structured interfaces
in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Prompt ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems").
Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 ([Team, 2025](#bib.bib28)) remains frozen
while executing sub-agent nodes. The generated graphs and patches are
canonicalized and validated before execution, and malformed or
unresolved outputs are handled as invalid actions. Following [Tsang et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib30), MAS-JudgeRM is trained by LoRA fine-tuning the
Qwen3-8B-based Skywork-Reward-V2 checkpoint with the Bradley-Terry
objective, using LoRA rank 32, scaling factor 64, and dropout 0.05.

|  Training batch size                    |  256                  |

## Appendix D Additional Ablation Experiments

We conduct three controlled studies to determine whether MAS-Loop’s
gains can be explained by additional MAS executions or an untrained
reflection pass, and whether the framework generalizes across base-model
scales.

### D.1 Rollout-Execution-Matched Training-Time MAS

To isolate the effect of additional MAS executions from
execution-grounded refinement, we increase the rollout group size of
MAS-Orchestra ([Ke et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)) from 16 to 32. MAS-Loop
executes 16 source MAS and 16 updated MAS per task, so this control
matches the number of executed MAS rollouts.

### D.2 One-Step Prompted Self-Reflection

We add a non-learned reflection control to distinguish the contribution
of the trained Refiner from the generic benefit of an additional
trajectory-conditioned inference pass. Given the task, source MAS, final
prediction, and the same gold-free execution trajectory available to
MAS-Loop, the Orchestrator is prompted once (i.e., using the
self-correction prompt ([He et al., 2025](#bib.bib56))) to diagnose the
execution and emit one revision under the same bounded operation
interface. The revised MAS is compiled and re-executed once. This
control therefore matches the source-revision-re-execution structure but
introduces no separately trained Refiner or coupled reward.

### D.3 Base-Model Scaling: Qwen3-14B

We replace Qwen3-8B with Qwen3-14B for both the Orchestrator and Refiner
while keeping the task data, policy interfaces, reward definitions,
rollout group size, frozen sub-agent backbone, executor, and evaluation
protocol unchanged. This comparison tests whether MAS-Loop generalizes
to a larger base model and can effectively convert increased policy
capacity into improved in-task and out-of-task performance.

| Training variant                        | HotpotQA | BCP_(OOT) |
|-----------------------------------------|----------|-----------|
| MAS-Loop                                | 64.50    | 15.48     |
| Rollout-execution-matched MAS-Orchestra | 54.00    | 12.50     |
| Orchestrator + one-step self-reflection | 59.50    | 11.90     |
| MAS-Loop with Qwen3-14B                 | 66.00    | 16.07     |

Table 5: Ablation results for rollout-execution matching, one-step
prompted self-reflection, and base-model scaling.

Analysis.
Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.3 Base-Model Scaling: Qwen3-14B ‣ Appendix D Additional Ablation Experiments ‣ MAS-Loop: Beyond One-Shot Orchestration towards Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems")
shows that the default MAS-Loop substantially outperforms
rollout-execution-matched MAS-Orchestra on both HotpotQA and BCP. Thus,
increasing the number of independently generated and executed MAS
rollouts alone does not recover the benefit of trajectory-conditioned
refinement. The self-correction results remain below MAS-Loop, isolating
the benefit of learning a dedicated Refiner rather than merely prompting
for an additional reflection pass. Replacing the trainable policies with
Qwen3-14B further improves MAS-Loop on both benchmarks, demonstrating
that the framework generalizes across base-model scales and benefits
from stronger policy backbones.

## Appendix E Case Study

We show one case from BrowseComp-Plus and compare the MAS produced by
Orchestrator and Refiner. The Orchestrator returns Northgate Market,
whereas the Refiner rewrote the role of agent_0 to require explicit
confirmation of the candidate’s presence in both Mexico and California.
This constraint discouraged premature selection based on the salient
California event clue alone and promoted a more complete evaluation of
the two-location condition. The revised evidence flow consequently
preserved Churrería El Moro as the candidate passed to downstream
aggregation, thus yielding the correct answer.
